dataset.name: Data from: "Moisture rivals temperature in limiting photosynthesis by trees establishing beyond their cold-edge range limit under ambient and warmed conditions"
description: This archive contains data files that were used to draw conclusions in “Moisture rivals temperature in limiting photosynthesis by trees establishing beyond their cold-edge range limit under ambient and warmed conditions”, by Moyes et al., 2015. All field research was completed in common garden plots set up as part of the Alpine Treeline Warming Experiment (ATWE) on Niwot Ridge, Colorado, USA.

There are two main data file formats in this archive: comma-separated values (.csv), and Microsoft Excel (.xls and .xlsx). .xlsx files can be read using Microsoft Excel and Google Sheets, and .csv files can be read using any simple text editor program, such as TextEdit (Mac) and Notepad (Windows). This .pdf data user’s guide can be read using Adobe Acrobat Reader, or any other compatible software. Seedling photographs and their corresponding leaf area-processed images are available in .jpg/.JPG image format, and can be opened using Preview (Mac) and Photos (Windows).

To provide additional spatial context, two types of geospatial files are also published in this data package: ESRI shapefiles (.shp) and .kml files. Shapefiles are compatible with any GIS software able to read the file type (such as QGIS or ESRI’s ArcGIS suite), and .kml files can be opened with Google Earth or Google Maps.

Figures 3 and 4 in the publication contain data from Moyes et al. 2013. This publication is cited in the References section in this archive, and data files can be accessed via the Alpine Treeline Warming Experiment project portal on ESS-DIVE.

- Climate change is altering plant species distributions globally, and warming is expected to promote uphill shifts in mountain trees. However, at many cold-edge range limits, such as alpine treelines in the western United States, tree establishment may be colimited by low temperature and low moisture, making recruitment patterns with warming difficult to predict.

- We measured response functions linking carbon (C) assimilation and temperature- and moisture-related microclimatic factors for limber pine (Pinus flexilis) seedlings growing in a heating × watering experiment within and above the alpine treeline. We then extrapolated these response functions using observed microclimate conditions to estimate the net effects of warming and associated soil drying on C assimilation across an entire growing season.

- Moisture and temperature limitations were each estimated to reduce potential growing season C gain from a theoretical upper limit by 15–30% (c. 50% combined). Warming above current treeline conditions provided relatively little benefit to modeled net assimilation, whereas assimilation was sensitive to either wetter or drier conditions.

- Summer precipitation may be at least as important as temperature in constraining C gain by establishing subalpine trees at and above current alpine treelines as seasonally dry subalpine and alpine ecosystems continue to warm.

spatialCoverage.description: Research was conducted within the Alpine Treeline Warming Experiment (ATWE), on Niwot Ridge in the Front Range of the Colorado Rocky Mountains, USA. The upper subalpine site (USA; 3430 m) is located on the upper-elevation edge of the subalpine forest, and is an open meadow surrounded by krummholz mats and flag trees. The site has a south-southwestern aspect, and has the highest snowpack due to snow being blown in and trapped from upwind.

The alpine site (ALP; 3540 m) is on Niwot Ridge and is located on a shallow southeastern slope approximately 400 m above timberline. The site is dominated by sedges, forbs, and grasses, and is characterized as an alpine meadow.

measurementTechnique:
Sites and experimental design
We conducted all work within the Alpine Treeline Warming Experiment (ATWE) at Niwot Ridge, Colorado, USA (Reinhardt et al., 2011; Castanha et al., 2012; Moyes et al., 2013). We utilized the treeline ecotone site (3430m) and the alpine site (3540 m), each containing 20 3-m-diameter common-garden plots. The treeline site was positioned at the elevation zone where tree growth becomes stunted to below 3m height, and the alpine site was above the elevation of established trees. Six infrared heaters (1000W each) surrounded each plot, using the geometry of Kimball et al. (2008), but with constant output (an estimated 170Wm^(- 2) under still conditions) from early March until early November. Heaters turned off when wind speed exceeded 30m s^(-1), measured at 2m height (03101-L; RM Young, Traverse City, MI, USA). Heating was crossed with a watering treatment, creating four treatment groups (control, watered, heated, heated and watered). Watered plots received 2.5mm water wk^(–1) starting 2–3 wk after snowmelt and continuing until the end of September. Mean annual precipitation (MAP) for Niwot Ridge is 808mm, and total precipitation during the 2012 water-year was 719mm, or 89% of MAP (NWCC, 2014).
To include potential genetic variability associated with elevation, we sowed locally collected (within 8 km of our sites) Pinus flexilis E. James seed from forest (3100 m) and treeline (3360 m) elevation sources (hereafter referred to as ‘provenances’) into separate 1 m^2 subplots in each common garden. We collected seed in autumn 2010 and sowed in clusters of five seeds at 10 cm spacing within subplots in October just before winter snow accumulated. Seeds germinated following snowmelt in 2011, and seedlings surviving into their second year (alive after snowmelt in 2012) formed the experimental cohort. Second-year seedlings developed true needles and began to shed their first-year cotyledons, but remained similar in stature to first-year seedlings.
Soil sensors (ECTM or 5TM; Decagon, Pullman, WA, USA; ATWE files used: d3_20130416), inserted vertically in the center of each subplot to integrate over 5–10 cm depth, measured temperature (Tsoil, °C) and volumetric water content (Θ, m^3 m^(-3)) every 15 min. We determined presence of snow cover from soil temperature as days with < 0.5°C diel Tsoil variability. We then identified snowmelt date for each subplot as the first snow-free day without subsequent snow cover lasting > 4 d.
We created a continuous approximation of seedling leaf temperature by estimating air temperature at 1 cm height above the soil surface (T1 cm) from Tsoil. We used T1 cm to approximate leaf temperature, because above-ground tissues of conifer seedlings of the size, age, and foliar morphology we evaluated have been generally shown to remain within c. 1°C of air temperature at 1 cm, owing to slender needles (Germino et al., 2002). We confirmed this at our sites by touching a fine-wire thermocouple to seedlings and comparing the result with surrounding air temperature on multiple dates. In addition, average wind speeds at 2 m for 2012 were 5.2 (treeline) and 7.9 m s^(-1) (alpine), with a very low frequency of wind speed measurements below 2 m s^(-1), especially during daylight hours. The short, uneven vegetation at these sites would have attenuated wind slightly (i.e. minimal zero plane displacement), and accounting for seedling morphology, we estimate an average leaf boundary layer thickness of c. 0.1 mm (Nobel, 2005). To generate the model, we measured T1 cm with thermocouples (type T) in four plots within each of the two sites, during three periods of 4–6 d in 2011, including days early and late in summer with relatively wet and dry soil. Thermocouple junctions were suspended beneath radiation shields and above the soil sensors. We then developed a model of T1 cm from Tsoil by adjusting diel soil temperature variability for differences in amplitude and phase at the surface. The T1 cm model reproduced measured T1 cm with an R^2 of 0.74 and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 3.41°C (See Fig. S1 in Supporting Information document)
Functional responses of net assimilation to microclimate gradients
To investigate limitations to net C assimilation associated with leaf temperature variability, we measured temperature response curves of net assimilation (Anet) at the treeline site in July and September 2012 (n = 23 total, Fig. 1 of publication). We measured Anet at saturating light (1200 μmol photons m^(-2) ^(s-1)) using a portable gas exchange system (6400XT with 2 x 3 cm leaf chamber and LED light source; Li-Cor Biosciences, Lincoln, NE, USA). During gas exchange measurements, we maintained reference CO2 at 400 μmol mol^(-1) and absolute humidity near ambient, and allowed time for stabilization as described by Moyes et al. (2013). We calculated gas flux densities relative to silhouette leaf area, determined using digital photos and image processing software (Image J; Scion, Fredrick, MD, USA). We first measured Anet at ambient temperature, and then we cooled seedlings to 8°C by using the chamber temperature control (Peltier coolers) and flowing ice water through heat exchange plates (6400- 88, Li-Cor Biosciences). We measured Anet again once chamber block temperature stabilized at 8°C or the lowest stable T achievable, and then at each 4°C step as we warmed seedlings incrementally to 30°C or the highest stable T achievable using the heating control.
We calculated temperature response curves of net assimilation for each seedling by fitting Anet to corresponding measurements of leaf temperature, after Säll & Pettersson (1994):
Anet(Tleaf) = Aopt-b(Tleaf–Topt)^2 Eqn 1.
Anet (Tleaf) was the fitted net assimilation function of Tleaf, and Aopt was the maximum net assimilation occurring at optimum temperature (Topt). The parameter b described the curvature of the parabolic fit, with larger b values associated with steeper declines in Anet as Tleaf deviated from Topt.
We assessed night-time maximum photosystem II (PSII) efficiency for evidence of photoinhibition, seedling midday stem water potential (indicative of low water balance), and associated midday Anet, during three campaigns at the alpine site and twice at the treeline site (Fig. 1). The treeline site was still buried in snow when the first alpine measurement set was collected (where only around half of plots were exposed). We assessed maximum PSII efficiency using either a portable fluorometer (MINI-PAM; Heinz Walz, Effeltrich Germany) or a photosynthesis chamber with fluorometer chamber attachment (6400-40; Li-Cor Biosciences) as the ratio of variable to maximum fluorescence elicited by low and saturating light (Fv/Fm) (Maxwell & Johnson, 2000). For both instruments, short segments (< 2 cm) of a few needles or cotyledons were pressed flat for measurement. Repeatability of measurements was confirmed by subsampling seedlings with both instruments. We collected fluorescence data at least 2 h after dusk to allow for dark acclimation. The total n sampled was 130 across sample dates (n = 30, 60, and 40 for campaigns 1, 2 and 3, respectively), sites (n = 50 at treeline, 80 at alpine), treatments (n = 25–42 per treatment), and provenances (n = 64 in the forest and 66 at treeline elevation). We revisited individuals sampled for fluorescence and measured daytime Anet (as earlier, using the 2 x 3 cm leaf chamber) between 09:00 and 16:00 h within 2 d of fluorescence measurements. Following gas exchange measurement, we excavated a subset of those individuals (n = 71) from the soil, severed the shoot, and assessed midday stem water potential (Ψ) using a pressure chamber (PMS-1000, PMS Instruments, OR, USA).
We used linear and nonlinear regression to relate physiological responses to microclimate variables derived from Tleaf, Tsoil, and Θ, using individual seedlings as replicates. It was not possible to replicate all measurements in all plots at all sampling points, owing to the presence of snow cover in some plots and unevenly distributed surviving seedlings. We used ANOVA to test for effects of heating, watering, and provenance on more evenly sampled temperature response parameters.
Model of daily and seasonal limitations to net assimilation
To estimate the relative importance of each microclimate factor on net assimilation under ambient and treatment conditions, we used soil sensor data to extrapolate observed Anet responses across all snow-free days and subplots within each site and treatment. We considered seedling C gain to be limited by microclimate conditions, such that:
Amax – Alim = Arealized Eqn 2.
where Amax is the light-saturated net assimilation rate under ideal microclimate conditions; Alim is the reduction of net assimilation by suboptimal microclimate effects; and Arealized is the net C assimilation during daylight hours within existing conditions, and represents the C available for growth of new tissue, respiration during night-time hours, storage in existing tissues, and losses via root exudation, litter, herbivory, etc.
We set maximum C assimilation (Amax) to 15μmol m^(-2) s^(-1) for daylight hours, because we measured this Anet flux density when temperature response curves and moisture sensitivity of gas exchange indicated that neither temperature nor moisture were limiting (see later). We used this maximum flux density, snowmelt and end-of-season dates, sunrise and sunset hours, and an average leaf area of 2 cm^2 to define an upper limit for seedling C assimilation. This upper limit was informative (e.g. revealing maximum effects of differences in snowmelt date on growing season assimilation), but entirely hypothetical, as photosynthesis rarely (if ever) operates without limitation; Amax merely represented an ideal upper bound for the purposes of comparing types of limitation. We regarded light as nonlimiting because extensive light response curves of seedlings at these sites (n > 80, not shown) have indicated that assimilation typically saturated below 400 μmol m^(-2) s^(-1), or around one-fifth of full sun.
We used the measured responses described earlier, and soil sensor data from each plot, to estimate the effect of four categories of Alim over the growing season. The categories were as follows: sub- or superoptimal leaf temperature; low soil moisture; cold-related PSII efficiency indicating photoinhibition; and repeated soil freezing (see Fig. S2 in Supporting Information for additional explanation of use of fitted response functions). Uncertainty in Alim associated with each category of limitation was calculated for each 15 min time step. We used Gaussian error propagation to combine sources of uncertainty at each model step, moving from microclimate inputs to Alim (arrows in Fig. S2, Supporting Information). We calculated uncertainty for each fitted response function as the standard error of the mean of residuals. We used the method of moments to calculate uncertainty in each functional response variable from uncertainty in input parameters. We used ANOVA to test for site, heating, and watering effects on each category of Alim expressed as a percentage of Amax integrated over the 2012 growing season.
